content: The ongoing challenge of managing multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) has driven the search for shorter and safer treatment regimens. In 2016, based on observational studies conducted in various Asian and African countries, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended, for the first time, a standardized 9-month treatment regimen. This regimen included an injectable agent and was significantly shorter than the existing standard of care, which typically lasted 18–20 months, for eligible patients. In 2018, following the results of the STREAM Stage 1 trial (Standard Treatment Regimen of Anti-tuberculosis Drugs for Patients with MDR-TB), modifications were made to the previously recommended shorter regimen. These changes included replacing kanamycin with amikacin, based on evidence comparing the effectiveness and safety of these two injectable agents. However, concerns about the permanent toxic effects of injectable agents have led to further advancements in developing injectable-sparing regimens. One notable development was the introduction of an all-oral, bedaquiline-containing 9-month regimen. Observational data from the South African Department of Health demonstrated the efficacy of this regimen, which was subsequently reviewed and recommended by WHO in 2019. The regimen included the following combination of medicines: 4–6 months of bedaquiline (Bdq), levofloxacin (Lfx) or moxifloxacin (Mfx), ethionamide (Eto), ethambutol (E), pyrazinamide (Z), high-dose isoniazid (Hh), and clofazimine (Cfz), followed by 5 months of Lfx (or Mfx), Cfz, Z, and E. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (Lzd, 600 mg). In 2019, data from the Nix-TB study, conducted by the Global TB Alliance, were reviewed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel 6-month regimen consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL). This regimen was designed to improve treatment outcomes for patients with MDR/RR-TB and additional resistance to fluoroquinolones. The study compared the BPaL regimen to matched records in the WHO Individual Patient Data (IPD) database. However, limitations in the study design, including a small sample size and observed adverse events, prevented the panel from recommending global programmatic implementation of the regimen until further evidence could be generated. In the 2020 WHO guidelines for drug-resistant TB, the BPaL regimen was recommended for use under operational research conditions. Two randomized controlled trials, TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, concluded in 2021, providing new evidence that prompted WHO to reassess and update its recommendations for MDR/RR-TB treatment. The ZeNix trial specifically compared two variations of the BPaL regimen: one using linezolid at 600 mg daily for 9 weeks (BPaL 600–9) and another using linezolid at 1200 mg daily for 26 weeks (BPaL 1200–26). Both regimens were tested in patients with MDR/RR-TB, with or without fluoroquinolone resistance. The trial found similar levels of treatment success, mortality, and resistance amplification between the two regimens. However, the BPaL 600–9 regimen showed a slightly increased risk of pretomanid monotherapy after week 9 in cases of undetected or unknown bedaquiline resistance. Additionally, follow-up data from the ZeNix trial revealed two additional treatment failures in the BPaL 600–9 arm after 12 months, compared to no additional failures in the other arms. The evidence from the ZeNix trial was judged to have very low certainty due to several factors. These included the small sample size, which introduced a high risk of imprecision, and imbalances in baseline characteristics such as prior TB treatment, smear status, and prevalence of fluoroquinolone resistance. Although the study was conducted in three countries (Russia, Moldova, and South Africa), which increased its generalizability, the small sample size and potential for unmeasured confounding led to downgrading the certainty of evidence. The panel also noted concerns about the high rates of adverse events associated with the 1200 mg dose of linezolid in the BPaL regimen, which could limit its programmatic implementation. Identifying the optimal dose and duration of linezolid within the BPaL regimen remains a priority to balance efficacy and safety. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted TB services worldwide, reversing years of progress. In 2020, there was an 18% decline in the number of newly diagnosed and reported TB cases, dropping to levels seen in 2012. This reduction in access to TB diagnosis and treatment has led to an increase in TB-related deaths, with a combined total of 1.5 million deaths in 2020, including 214,000 among HIV-positive individuals. The number of people receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB also fell by 15% between 2019 and 2020, with only about one-third of those in need receiving treatment. Despite these challenges, there have been improvements in treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB. Globally, the treatment success rate increased from 50% in 2012 to 59% in 2018, reflecting steady progress. However, drug-resistant TB remains a global challenge, with treatment regimens often being long, toxic, and expensive. The development of more effective and shorter regimens is essential to optimize treatment outcomes, minimize adverse events, and prevent the acquisition of additional drug resistance. The BPaL regimen is currently recommended by WHO for the treatment of patients with MDR/RR-TB and fluoroquinolone resistance under operational research conditions. However, the high rates of adverse events associated with the 1200 mg dose of linezolid remain a concern. Further research is needed to determine the optimal dose and duration of linezolid to ensure both efficacy and safety.
